title: Course framework + Rydin (2021) Introduction: Theory and planning research
one: Theory is not optional: every definition of 'planning' already frames the object. A theory (ontology + epistemology + values) tells you what to focus on, links your case to a broader story, and lets research build theory. The course compares theories on four dimensions.
summary: Rydin (2021) writes about theory OF planning (analytic: how planning works), not normative planning theory FOR planning (how it should be done), while admitting the two are entangled: 'all research—including analytic research—is imbued with value judgements'. Even defining planning is theoretical: planning as goal-directed decision-making (instrumental, public administration, e.g. Næss & Saglie 2000) → as state action to order the environment in the collective interest → as intervention affecting diverse interests and system features. Each small shift implies a different view of the process.

Knowledge is more than information: it is about understanding the dynamics that produced a situation, 'a claim to know the cause of things' (rerum cognoscere causas). Research combines general understanding with a specific case. Theory can be seen as law-like (natural-science model; rejected by Flyvbjerg et al. 2012 because of complexity and Giddens' double hermeneutic) or, Rydin's view, as 'a heuristic aid to understanding a situation, a way to try to know what is essentially unknowable in its completeness' (p. 9): 'a set of ideas that fit together coherently and make general statements about the world or a part of it'. Theories carry ontological, normative and epistemological positions, so the terrain of theory is contested and choosing one is a value choice.

Is theory necessary? Empiricism ('let the facts speak', Latour's 'modernist settlement') fails: data selection and interpretation involve value judgements, and pure empiricism gives a disparate, unconnected field. Flyvbjerg's phronesis (practical wisdom; four questions: where are we going, who gains/loses by which mechanisms of power, is it desirable, what should we do?) still relies on unacknowledged theory (double hermeneutic, praxis). Three advantages of theory: (1) it focuses attention under time/money limits; (2) it links partial findings to a broader, persuasive narrative, enabling generalisation; (3) empirical research can build and revise theory.

The course then compares theories on four dimensions: (1) sources of planning outcomes (structure ↔ agency); (2) reproduction and change (reproduction ↔ transformation; deliberate ↔ emergent); (3) knowledge (universal ↔ situated; monist ↔ pluralist; + realism ↔ relativism); (4) normative commitments. Theories make explanatory, evaluative and prescriptive claims. Rydin's book runs from the linear rational model (ch. 2), through actor-centred approaches (rational choice, institutions, governance, urban politics; chs 3–6) and structural political economy (ch. 7), to relational perspectives (Foucault, assemblage; chs 8–9).
concepts: A heuristic aid; a coherent set of ideas making general statements about (part of) the world; a narrative account, never complete.
Theory of vs theory for planning
Analytic (how planning works) vs normative (how it should be done) (Faludi's distinction).
'Let the facts speak for themselves': rejected because data choice and interpretation are value-laden and findings stay disconnected.
Flyvbjerg's practical-wisdom research: situated, value-deliberative, attentive to power. Rydin: it still hides theoretical choices.
Social scientists interpret how people interpret the world (Giddens), so social science ≠ natural science.
Focus; link to a broader narrative (generalisation); build/revise theory.
Patterned arrangements limiting choice / capacity to act independently.
How it works / whether it is good / what to do.
Assumption about what ought to be valued, pursued, protected.
example: A thesis asking 'which municipal instrument best raises housing output?' assumes a deliberate, planner-centred, universal-knowledge view (governmental model). A thesis asking 'how do tenant groups' experiences of renovation differ?' assumes situated, pluralist knowledge.

examples.d: Rydin notes that the same data on housebuilding rates can support different narratives depending on whether you take a historical view, focus on housebuilders' behaviour, or on planners' decisions and their rationale. Shows why empiricism fails: data never 'speaks for itself', so a theoretical framing is needed to pick and defend one narrative.

If a phronetic researcher works with political leaders to change planning through dialogue, that assumes change comes via feedback or communicative action; if they help community groups in planning disputes, that assumes planning is a conflict-ridden political process. Shows Rydin's point that phronesis still relies on an unacknowledged theoretical choice.

Governance theory (analytic, from political science) explains policy through stakeholder networks, while collaborative planning theory (normative) wants more communicative action between those same stakeholders. Shows that theory OF planning and theory FOR planning overlap even though Rydin's book stays on the analytic side.

Lecture case: a landowner offers 2,000 market-rate homes that comply with the rules and need no subsidy, while the city considers 1,600 homes with 40% affordable, priority for low-income households and a EUR 50 million public contribution. Shows that normative commitments decide what counts as the problem and what you measure when judging which plan is better.

title: Buitelaar (2026) Making sense of The Just City
one: 'The Just City' is a concept everyone supports, but its conceptions differ: the Happy, Equal, Supportive and Free City. Each has different materials of justice and policies, and they are not à la carte: some are internally or externally incongruent. Planners need 'justice literacy'.
summary: Concept vs conception (Moroni 2020, after Rawls): nobody opposes the concept of a just city, but conceptions differ. Three problems in debates: justice kept vague to avoid controversy (superficial consensus); justice defined narrowly as if only one conception exists (e.g. Fainstein's anti-neoliberal framing); and inconsistency when incompatible conceptions are pursued at once (you can't condemn segregation and gentrification AND support free settlement). Aim: improve 'justice literacy', i.e. the vocabulary (conceptions) and grammar (how they connect).

Premises: strictly, a city cannot be just; only institutions (formal and informal rules) can (Moroni). 'City' = the target territory where goods, duties or rights are allocated. Each conception decomposes into five materials of justice (Dawkins 2021): value (what is distributed), principle (how), scope (to whom/where), ground (why), basis (goal-based vs rights/duty-based).

Happy City (utilitarianism): value = utility/preference satisfaction; principle = maximum collective utility; goal-based. Policies: CBA, agglomeration economies (often labelled 'neoliberal'). Critique: ignores distribution and individual rights. Equal City (egalitarianism): value = equality of outcomes/opportunities; 'the more equal, the better'; inequality instrumentally problematic (neighbourhood effects) and intrinsically wrong. Policies: redistribution, social mixing. Supportive City (sufficientarianism, + prioritarianism, limitarianism): everyone ENOUGH (absolute, not relative poverty); access to primary goods/capabilities, e.g. affordable housing (≤30% of income), commuting limits; setting the threshold is key; rights/duty-based. Free City (liberalism; Hayek, Nozick): equal rights and freedom; 'assigning rights rather than distributing outcomes'; the city as spontaneous order; Nozick's entitlement theory (justice in acquisition and transfer); refrain from growth controls, inclusionary zoning, rent control; Oosterwold. A positive-freedom variant: the capability approach (Sen, Nussbaum).

Congruence: internal = do the materials within one conception fit (e.g. utility + individual rights don't)? External = do conceptions fit each other? Free + Supportive can combine (primary goods can be rights; capabilities fit sufficiency). The Free City is incompatible with the goal-based Happy and Equal Cities: formal equality clashes with material equality, and 'liberty upsets patterns' (Nozick), e.g. free settlement produces clustering. 'Justice is not à la carte.'
concepts: The general idea of justice vs a specific version of it.
Knowing the vocabulary (conceptions) and grammar (connections) of justice.
Aims at an end-state for the collective (Happy, Equal) vs secures rights/duties (Supportive, Free).
Utilitarian; maximum collective utility; CBA, agglomeration.
Egalitarian; everyone the same (relative); social mixing, redistribution.
Sufficientarian; everyone enough (absolute); spatial primary goods such as affordable housing.
Liberal; equal rights and freedom; refrain from intervening; Oosterwold; capabilities (positive freedom).
Fit between materials within one conception / between conceptions.
A distribution is just if it came about through just acquisition and transfer.
example: Amsterdam's rule that new developments include a fixed share of social housing combines the Equal City (mixing) and the Supportive City (enough affordable homes). A Free City critic would call it a restriction of property rights; a Happy City analyst would run a CBA.

examples.d: To set a sufficiency threshold for housing, Buitelaar cites the room stress factor (rooms available divided by rooms required, minus 1; below 0 is inadequate) and the 30% housing ratio, which he says says little without absolute income, hence the 'budget approach'. Shows that in the Supportive City the key task is defining and measuring the threshold.

Refusing mortgages because a home is in a marginalised neighbourhood or postcode, regardless of the applicant's borrowing capacity, is unjust from a liberal view because it breaches equal rights. Shows the Free City's rules: negative and universal (Hayek's 'negative test of universality'), removing unjust conduct rather than steering outcomes.

An investor who legitimately buys and rents out many properties ends up owning far more than owner-occupiers; eyebrows may be raised, but for liberalism this is no injustice. Shows Nozick's entitlement theory: a distribution is just if acquisition and transfer were legitimate, whatever pattern results.

A bike is a commodity, the pleasure of riding it is utility, but what counts is the capability to ride it or choose not to; for a disabled person the bike itself is of little use. Shows the capability approach (positive freedom) and why it departs from resource-based conceptions like Rawls's primary goods.

title: Hall (2014/2020) The City of Theory
one: After 1955 planning became an academic discipline and swung from craft (design) to science (systems/rational planning), then fragmented (Lindblom, Davidoff, Marxists, communicative theory), and in the process lost its 'priestly clothing'.
summary: Before 1955 planning was an extension of architecture and engineering: design-based, blueprint end-state plans, survey–analysis–plan (Geddes), with 'theory in planning but no theory of planning'. Goals were implicit, the planner 'would get it right first time', and the political environment was passive: Batty calls it planning's golden age (e.g. Abercrombie's static city with a green belt).

The 1950s baby boom, economic boom and mass car ownership overwhelmed that static system. At the same time a 'quantitative revolution' (location theory: von Thünen, Weber, Christaller, Lösch; Isard's regional science) and cybernetics (Wiener) arrived. 1960–70: the systems revolution. Cities are systems to be modelled, monitored and controlled (McLoughlin, Chadwick; transportation studies Detroit 1955, Chicago 1956; Lowry model). Rational planning is the theory of the process (Faludi), systems planning the theory of the object. Planning becomes a science, not an art.

From 1965 to 1975 critiques 'stripped the planner of whatever priestly clothing' he or she had: from the right/pluralists (Lindblom's muddling through; Meyerson & Banfield; Altshuler) and from the left (Davidoff's advocacy planning; Arnstein). Rittel & Webber's wicked problems undercut optimal solutions. Then came the Marxist ascendancy (Harvey, Massey, Castells, Lefebvre): planning serves the reproduction of capital and labour, so planning theory is a product of social forces, a logic Hall calls 'strangely quietist'. Forester tries to resolve it with Habermas: communicative action. Hall's jab: stripped of its philosophy, it is 'good old-fashioned democratic common sense', i.e. Davidoff again. Theory and practice: honeymoon in the 1960s, tiffs in the 1970s, divorce in the 1980s.
concepts: Pre-1955: design-based, blueprint, end-state plans, intuitive expert goals.
Theory in vs theory of planning
Borrowed snippets of theory about cities vs a theory of what planning (the process) is.
Theory of the object: the city as a system of interrelated activities in flux, monitored and controlled (cybernetics).
Theory of the process: goals → inventory → model → forecast → alternatives → evaluation → choice → monitoring (Faludi 1973).
The planner's special status and mystique as expert, lost 1965–75.
Planning is a function of the capitalist state: it secures accumulation and reproduction of labour, and always solves one problem by creating another.
Forester (via Habermas): planning as communicative action that can distort or reveal; later Healey, Innes. Rydin (2007) calls it the 'new orthodoxy'.
Drawing board → analysing computer output → talking to community groups in the evenings (Hall, p. 386).
example: The Dutch Vinex-era models and MKBA practice are the 1960s systems/rational legacy still alive; a participatory 'omgevingsdialoog' under the Omgevingswet is the communicative legacy.

examples.d: Hall's caricature: in 1955 the new planner sat at the drawing board drawing land uses, in 1965 analysed computer output of traffic patterns, and in 1975 talked late into the night with community groups. Shows the shift from craft to systems science to advocacy, and the loss of the planner's claim to unique expertise.

Altshuler found the professional planner had no clout against the political machine, which backed the highway engineers; they won by stressing expertise and narrow goals. Shows the pluralist critique from the right: real decisions are political, far from the 'cool, rational, Olympian' style of the systems texts.

Marxists argued planning always solves one problem by creating another: 19th-century clearances in Paris created a working-class housing problem, and American zoning limited industrialists' most profitable locations. Shows the Marxist view that planning can modify but never remove the contradiction between private accumulation and collective action.

The knowledge lecture illustrates 'planning as a craft' with Berlage's Plan Zuid for Amsterdam (1904/1915): a detailed, aesthetic blueprint plan. Shows the pre-1955 design tradition where there was theory in planning but no theory of planning.

title: Rydin (2007) Re-examining the role of knowledge within planning theory
one: Modernist planning reified knowledge as an object; postmodern planning celebrates many knowledges but has no institutional arrangements to handle them. Rydin argues for treating knowledge as claims about causal relations, distinguishing them from other (ethical, aesthetic) claims, and creating arenas where planners open up to and test (close down) them.
summary: Starting point: the breakdown of the modernist consensus (Latour): knowledge is not a mirror of nature produced by neutral experts, but socially constructed and embedded in social relations and networks (epistemic communities, communities of practice). Modernist planning rested on planners' command of knowledge for progress. Knowledge differs from information and data because it specifies a causal relationship: planners need to know how impacts follow from actions.

The 'new orthodoxy' in planning theory (consensus building: Innes; collaborative: Healey; radical: Sandercock's 'epistemology of multiplicity') places knowledge outside planning organisations. But deliberation has limits: general ones (vague practice, planner skills, capture by powerful interests, unresolved conflict) and knowledge-specific ones: knowledges are not additive (Evans & Marvin); Innes's consensus building works when information is fully shared or 'uncertainty is rampant', whereas most planning lies in between. 'Engaging different knowledges is fundamentally different to engaging different voices.'

Knowledge claims must be distinguished from ethical, pragmatic, efficiency or aesthetic claims, since stakeholder rights ≠ expertise rights (Collins & Evans). Habermas's validity claims support this: truth (constatives), normative legitimacy (regulatives), truthfulness (expressives). Labelling all community claims 'knowledge' is politically understandable but wrong: experience 'is not of itself a sufficient condition for it to be knowledge' (p. 9 of MS / p. 56). Planners are co-producers of knowledge (Mode 2): they give voice (opening up) AND test and recognise claims (closing down), aiming at 'socially robust knowledge'. This is a realist constructivism: knowledge is socially constructed yet engages material reality.

Typology (Figure 1): planning seeks to turn State A into B1; without planning A becomes B; the actual result is B2. Seven knowledge types: (1) empirical State A, (2) predictive State B, (3) process A→B, (4) process A→B1 (how planning works), (5) empirical B2 (outcomes), (6) process A→B2, (7) normative B1 (desired future, normative yet grounded in possible paths). Collapsed into four: empirical, process, predictive, normative (Table 2). None is value-free and each carries a causal story. Each type needs different arenas and planner roles: empirical = lay + expert, planner as client, analyst or facilitator; process = theory-framed research, even action research; predictive = mostly expert-led, planner as client; normative = public-sphere debate, planners keep possible futures on the table (an ethical voice).
concepts: A claim specifying causal relationships, not just data or information.
Knowledge as an objective mirror of nature produced by experts; its breakdown = knowledge as socially constructed.
Communicative/collaborative planning: many stakeholders, many knowledges, consensus.
Knowledge claims differ from ethical, pragmatic, efficiency and aesthetic claims (Habermas's validity claims; Collins & Evans).
Give voice to claims; test and recognise which count as knowledge.
Planners help generate knowledge by testing and recognising claims.
Empirical, predictive, process (×3), normative → empirical, process, predictive, normative.
Does validity depend on who produced the claim and from where?
How many independent sources can confer the status of knowledge?
Can claims be judged against each other? Rydin: soft relativism, but claims can be tested.
Several disciplines (can still be monist) vs non-academics as knowledge producers (pluralist).
example: Grenfell Tower: the Grenfell Action Group's warnings (local experiential knowledge) were ignored. Opening up would have heard them; closing down would have tested them against fire-safety evidence.

examples.t: B, B1 and B2 in housing
examples.d: Rydin's own illustration: B is the expected housing shortage, B1 the planned match of supply and need, and B2 the actual result of profitable developments alongside continued overcrowding, housing stress and homelessness. Shows why planning needs outcome (B2) and process knowledge, not just knowledge of the goal.

Experts often present a community's view of an environmental risk as exaggerated, yet local experience such as episodes of ill-health can be a basis to challenge the expert assessment. Rydin adds that not all community risk perceptions are therefore knowledge, so shows the need to separate knowledge claims from other claims and test them (closing down).

Describing an area's affluence with market prices or with child poverty makes a difference. Shows that even descriptive (empirical) knowledge is value-laden in its framing and carries an implicit causal story.

Lecture exercise: 'car ownership in Utrecht fell by 12% (2015-2023)' is empirical; 'housing demand in Rijnenburg will exceed supply by 2030' is predictive; 'densification near stations reduces car dependency' and 'participation produces better plans' are process claims; 'Rijnenburg should prioritise affordability over aesthetics' is normative. Shows how Rydin's typology tells you which arena and test each claim needs.

title: Marx (1844) Estranged Labour
one: Under capitalism workers are estranged from their product, their activity, their species-being and each other. History is driven by class struggle over the means of production, so real change needs a structural change of the base: abolition of private property.
summary: Humans realise themselves through labour, their transformative relation with nature. Under private property and wage labour this relation is inverted: 'The worker becomes all the poorer the more wealth he produces.' Marx names four estrangements: from the product (it confronts him as an alien power), from the act of production (labour is 'not voluntary, but coerced; it is forced labor'), from species-being (conscious creative activity reduced to a means to survive) and from other humans.

Private property is the 'product, the result, the necessary consequence, of alienated labor', though it then reproduces it. An enforced increase of wages would be 'nothing but better payment for the slave' and would not restore human significance to labour.

Lecture framing: Marx adapts Hegel's dialectic but replaces 'the Spirit' with material relations (historical materialism). The base (means and relations of production) determines the superstructure (values, norms, ideology). This is a deterministic view: humans are subject to, not actors of, broad change. Politically this becomes revolution: abolish private property, pass through a socialist state towards a stateless society. For planning: markets produce material inequality by design, so the progressive planner plans for the poor and the working class through decommodified models (Madden & Marcuse 2016).
concepts: Four forms: from the product, from the labour process, from species-being, from other people.
The human capacity for conscious, free, purposeful creative activity.
The material base (means and relations of production) drives history and shapes the superstructure.
Economy and property relations / ideology, law, culture, norms.
History as the clash of opposites: owners vs the disowned (class struggle).
Land, factories, tools; ownership defines class.
Turning things (labour, housing, land) into goods produced for exchange value, not use value.
example: HC4 slide, quoting Madden & Marcuse (2016): overcrowding and unaffordable homes 'are not market failures, they are how the market works'. The answer is decommodified housing (public, cooperative), not a tweak of zoning.

examples.d: HC4 slides: with the shift from an agricultural to an industrial economy, workers no longer transformed matter for their own use but commodified their bodies for a small wage. Shows estrangement from the product and from the act of production.

The slide quotes Marx: an enforced rise in wages would be nothing more than better pay for slaves and would not raise human significance or dignity. Shows the structural argument: fixing outcomes within wage labour and private property does not end alienation, only changing the base does.

The slides quote Lenin that the state must persist until capitalist resistance is crushed and there are no classes, as the step from capitalist state to socialist state to stateless society. Shows the deliberate, structure-changing route to material equality in Marxist thought.

Between the wars the Social Democratic city government of Vienna built tens of thousands of municipal flats at low rents, such as the Karl-Marx-Hof (1927-1930). Shows decommodified housing in the Madden and Marcuse sense, though as reform within capitalism rather than Marx's abolition of private property.

title: Hayek (1944) Planning and democracy
one: Central economic planning directs all of society towards a single goal, which presupposes a 'complete ethical code' that nobody has. Because democratic assemblies can agree that there should be a plan but not on its ends, planning shifts decisions to experts and discretion, and ultimately to dictatorship. Democracy only works when collective action is limited to fields where true agreement exists and power is bound by general rules.
summary: Starting point (pp. 42–44): all collectivism (communism, fascism) is 'the deliberate organisation of the labours of society for a definite social goal'. Goals such as the 'common good' or 'general welfare' are too vague to decide any concrete action; a single plan would need every need of every person ranked in one order of values, i.e. a 'complete ethical code'. No such code exists: as civilisation grew, moral rules became fewer and more general, merely marking out a sphere of individual freedom. Nobody can survey more than a limited field of needs, so only partial, mutually inconsistent scales of values exist, in individual minds. That, not egoism, is the basis of individualism: the individual is 'the ultimate judge of his ends'.

Limits of common action (pp. 44–45): social ends are just the identical ends of many individuals, so common action must be limited to fields where people agree; agreement is likeliest on means that serve many purposes, and its probability falls as the scope of state action widens. Once the state controls a large enough share of resources (Germany 1928: 53% of national income), it indirectly controls almost everything, and the 'social scale of values' must cover nearly all individual ends.

The democratic mechanism (pp. 45–51): people may agree on planning without agreeing on its ends, like a group committing to a journey without agreeing where to go. Parliaments then fail and are seen as 'talking shops'; planning is 'taken out of politics' and delegated to experts (Hayek quotes the Webbs, Laski and the Donoughmore Committee). Majority voting suits choices between limited alternatives, but a plan needs 'a unitary conception' and cannot be voted clause by clause. Unlike a general with one goal, the planner must choose between competing ends, so experts impose their own scale of preferences. Delegation of general rule-making (even to local authorities) is acceptable; delegation of discretion in particular cases ('judging the case on its merits') creates arbitrary power. Separate sectoral plans do not add up, the cry for an 'economic dictator' follows, and parliament ends up choosing persons with near-absolute power: 'plebiscitarian dictatorship'. Germany before 1933 is the example: Hitler exploited a democracy that had already decayed.

Conclusion (pp. 51–53): 'It is the price of democracy' that conscious control is limited to fields of true agreement and some things are left to chance. The liberal creed reduced the range of subjects needing agreement; only within a competitive system based on free disposal over private property is democracy possible. Democracy is not an end but 'a utilitarian device' for peace and freedom; a homogeneous majority can be oppressive. Planning leads to dictatorship because dictatorship is the most effective instrument of coercion. What prevents arbitrary power is 'not the source but the limitation of power'.

Slides vs chapter: the lecture presents Hayek through spontaneous order, indeterminism, 'the theory of complex phenomena' (cited as Hayek 1989) and equality of rights vs Marx's material equality. None of these terms appears in this chapter. Dispersed local knowledge comes from Hayek (1945) 'The use of knowledge in society' (cited by Cozzolino); spontaneous order (kosmos vs taxis) from Law, Legislation and Liberty (1973; Moroni cites the 1982 edition). The chapter itself argues from value pluralism, the limits of any one mind's view of needs and ends, and the political mechanics of majority rule and delegation. The slide headings 'The philosophy of individualism' and 'Planning in democracy' are the parts actually drawn from this chapter.
concepts: 'The deliberate organisation of the labours of society for a definite social goal' (p. 42); denies autonomous spheres where individual ends are supreme.
A ranking of all human values complete enough to decide every choice a central plan requires; Hayek says it does not exist (pp. 43–44).
Not egoism: because no mind can survey more than a sector of society's needs, the individual should be the ultimate judge of his own ends within defined limits (p. 44).
Common action is legitimate where individual views coincide; agreement falls as the scope of state action grows (p. 45).
When assemblies cannot agree on a plan, it is handed to experts, who then impose their own scale of preferences (pp. 46–48).
Delegating general rule-making is acceptable; delegating decisions on particular cases 'on their merits' produces arbitrary power (p. 49).
End state of democratic planning: parliament only confirms a leader who holds practically absolute power (p. 51).
Conscious control restricted to fields of true agreement; 'in some fields things must be left to chance' (p. 51).
'A utilitarian device for safeguarding internal peace and individual freedom' (p. 52), not the highest end.
example: The chapter's own cases: Germany, where by 1928 public authorities controlled 53% of national income and democracy had in effect broken down before 1933, so 'Hitler did not have to destroy democracy' (p. 50); and Britain, where Laski proposed governing by delegated legislation and Order in Council (pp. 46–47). Planning illustration (not in the text): a permit system that decides each project 'on its merits' is what Hayek calls discretion; a zoning code of general rules is the acceptable form.

examples.d: People agreeing on central planning without agreeing on its ends are like a group committing to travel together without agreeing where to go, so most end up on a journey they do not want. Shows Hayek's claim that agreement exists only on the mechanism, which pushes decisions to experts.

A general can be handed one supreme goal for a campaign, but an economic planner must choose between the conflicting ends of different people, so experts end up imposing their own scale of preferences. Shows why delegating planning is not just delegating technical detail.

Halevy suggested a composite photograph of Eustace Percy, Oswald Mosley and Stafford Cripps would show one shared feature: the belief that only dictatorial leadership could end economic chaos. Shows Hayek's 'cry for an economic dictator' as a stage on the road from planning to plebiscitarian dictatorship.

The HC4 slide pairs Hayek with Glaeser and Gyourko (2003): zoning strictness correlates with high prices, a few subsidised units barely affect prices, but cutting the 'zoning tax' on new construction could have a massive impact. Shows the liberal planner's role: set a level framework rather than limit supply or steer outcomes.

title: Cozzolino (2020) The (anti) adaptive neighbourhoods
one: Cities as a whole are complex adaptive systems, but many 20th-century neighbourhoods built all at once are anti-adaptive. The cause lies in neglected factors: action (the source of change), ownership (which distributes design control) and time. Planners should create room for incremental, self-organised adaptation instead of more central plans.
summary: AANs = large residential neighbourhoods built all-at-once and from scratch in the 20th century (e.g. 'La Clementina', Bergamo, vs historic 'Borgo Santa Caterina'). They answered housing pressures and gave affordable ownership, but they are 'in a lock-in situation': they can't self-regenerate, so they call for top-down, 'paternalistic' regeneration. Aims: characterise the causes of AAN formation and perpetuation, and give policy/design implications. Adaptability matters for persistence, identity and innovation (use of dispersed local knowledge, Hayek, Jacobs).

Traditional cities grew from private ownership, incremental development and organic adjustment among households, governed by legal codes that protected neighbours. Modern planning shifted from proscriptive rules ('thou shalt not', only preventing externalities) to prescriptive rules that predefine spatial configurations. Complexity is emergent (spontaneous action); simplicity is designed: 'the more one neighbourhood is designed from the top, the less space there is for complexity to evolve'.

Planning's direct responsibility: pushing large-scale developments, demanding large public open spaces, and rules that freeze adaptation. Implications: include time (after construction, leave room for unpredictable adaptation); use 'locality knowledge' while preventing negative externalities; welcome multiple independent ownerships and distributed design control ('everything depends on the pattern of ownership', Moudon). Regeneration: abandon paternalism. New areas: top-down design only for certain common structures; Oosterwold as an experiment. Final point: the problem isn't too few central plans but 'the lack of flexible space for incremental adaptation and the evolution of self-organized orders'. Not nostalgic: the focus is 'the institutional framework that shaped [the traditional city's] evolutionary process', and a distance from New Urbanism.
concepts: Built all-at-once from scratch, reluctant to incremental change, 'lock-in'.
The three under-estimated factors behind adaptability.
Prohibitions preventing externalities vs rules predefining spatial outcomes.
Emergent order from spontaneous action vs designed artificial order: a trade-off.
Ownership as the legal title that spreads design control among many actors.
Jacobs: people's situated knowledge of their own needs and place.
AANs can't self-regenerate, so top-down interventions follow, which reproduce dependence.
example: Oosterwold (Almere): buyers get a plot and a short list of rules (build on max. 20%, grow food, arrange your own road and utilities) instead of a master plan.

examples.d: Cozzolino notes that recreating the physical pattern of the traditional city today would be blocked by prescriptions such as minimum road widths, building distances, parking and green-space standards. Shows the shift from proscriptive rules ('thou shalt not') to prescriptive rules that lower adaptive capacity.

In 2015, self-building made up only 10-15% of new housing in the Netherlands and the UK, even though they are seen as leading nations. Shows demand-driven development and distributed design control as the alternative to supply-driven, all-at-once large projects, and how marginal it still is.

Because of preservation policies and restrictive rules, old historic quarters sometimes show the typical problems of an AAN. Shows that anti-adaptiveness comes from rules and design control, not from age or form, and raises the question whether preservation and adaptability can be reconciled.

Listed by Cozzolino among Europe's AANs (note 1), the Bijlmermeer was built in one go from the late 1960s as high-rise honeycomb blocks with large collective green space; from the 1990s a top-down renewal demolished part of it and added low-rise, more often owner-occupied homes. Shows the lock-in and the costly central regeneration ('paternalistic circle') that AANs tend to need.

title: Rydin (2021) Governmental models: the hope of rational public administration
one: The governmental model frames planning as a rational, linear (with feedback) process in which politicians set goals and expert planners choose the best means. Research within it becomes policy evaluation: 'a critical friend shadowing the steps'.
summary: Justification comes from welfare economics: markets fail through externalities, missing markets (information), public and merit goods and monopoly (including landowners'), so the public sector intervenes in the public interest. The public interest in this view is the greatest net benefit to society, and planning is welfare optimisation.

In the Weberian tradition goals 'stand outside the planning process'. Politicians set ends; public administration brings 'expert knowledge to bear on the options available'. The ideal process is Lichfield et al.'s (1975) eleven steps, from problem definition to review. Four features: (1) evidence-based planning, where knowledge 'can be gathered and made available to the planning process in a positive way' (p. 22); (2) a comprehensive synthesis across all dimensions (triple bottom line, systems thinking à la McLoughlin); legitimacy 'comes from the rationality of the analysis' (p. 24); tools such as EA/SEA, CBA, MCA and GIS inform but do not decide; (3) formulation to implementation, with policy instruments (direct investment, strategic spatial planning, regulation, fiscal measures, tradeable permits, information/nudges); (4) implementation studies show how tools are used matters, planners exercise discretion and negotiate, and the politics/administration line blurs.

Critiques from the lecture: wicked problems (Rittel & Webber 1973), incrementalism/muddling through (Lindblom 1959), advocacy planning (Davidoff 1965). Its ideal-typical assumptions are complete information, clear agreed goals, and objective value-free decisions separated from politics. Yet 'rationality is dead but keeps showing up' (Brooks 2002): e.g. the Dutch MKBA (social cost-benefit analysis) of the toll-free Westerscheldetunnel (net welfare gain €27–39m, ratio 1.5, but 'the feeling of injustice about the toll' could not be priced).
concepts: Choosing the most efficient means for given ends; planning = optimisation.
Politicians set goals; trained officials apply impersonal rules and expertise to choose means.
Externalities, missing markets, public goods, merit goods, monopoly; justifies planning (welfare economics).
Problem definition → decision to act → data/forecast → constraints/objectives → criteria → design → test alternatives → evaluate → decide → implement → review.
Integrating all dimensions of a problem into one balanced view; source of legitimacy.
'we can make policies work better if we understand how policy mechanisms bring about change' (Sanderson 2002).
How tools are used; discretion and negotiation; goals reformulated during implementation.
Research within this model mirrors the model: evaluation of steps, goals taken as given.
Dutch social cost-benefit analysis: compares options with a no-policy future, in euros where possible.
example: Westerscheldetunnel toll: MKBA says abolishing the toll gives a net gain of €27–39m (B/C 1.5), but it cannot price the felt injustice, so politicians still decide.

examples.t: Energy planning in Escamp, The Hague
examples.d: Hettinga et al. piloted a Geodesign decision support system in Escamp with 12 municipal sustainability officers, a touch table and real-time impact assessments, ending in three agreed boundary conditions and a neighbourhood energy plan. Shows the governmental model's decision-support theme: better data and tools help planners choose the best means, with stakeholders involved instrumentally.

The official self-assessment found 19 of 22 indicator targets for 2014 met, but Ma et al.'s broader evaluation matrix found no sustainable transport, poor waste sorting and little gain for residents. Shows implementation and evaluation research that still judges outcomes against the plan itself (plan implementation).

examples.t: Tourism scheme at Ria de Aveiro
examples.d: A 309-home tourism development on a lagoon sandbar in Portugal was scaled down after EIA negotiations, then refused when a new national government's commission raised coastal erosion. Pinho uses it to show discretion and negotiation inside the planning steps, and how separated procedures block the integrated, balanced view the model promises.

The lecture shows Dutch post-war social housing (1945-1965), when the ministry's 'Voorschriften en Wenken' decided centrally what a home should be. An example of the governmental model institutionalised: experts fix the right means for politically given housing goals.

title: Scott (1998/2020) The high-modernist city
one: High-modernist planning (Le Corbusier, CIAM, Brasília, Chandigarh) imposed a legible, geometric, functionally segregated order seen from above. It produced visual order but social failure, and an unplanned city at the margins. Jane Jacobs's street-level view shows real order is complex and experienced.
summary: High modernism = a strong belief in scientific and technical progress, rational design of the social order, and state power to impose it (with a weak civil society). Le Corbusier's 'total city planning': a tabula rasa, geometry and standardisation (right angles, the straight line), strict functional segregation (work, home, leisure, traffic), and 'rule by the plan, the planner, and the state': the plan is to be imposed, with no consultation. He saw the city from the air; the plan was a utopian project, legible and easy to police.

Brasília (Costa and Niemeyer, under Kubitschek) is 'the closest thing we have to a high-modernist city'. It was built from zero on state land as a 'utopian miniaturization' meant to transform Brazil. Residents got 'brasilite': no street corners, no crowds, uniform superquadra blocks, disorientation. Legibility for administrators meant confusion for residents. By 1980, 75% of the population lived in unplanned settlements; the planned city depended on the unplanned one ('symbiotic'). Chandigarh (Le Corbusier) repeated this: monumental axes, empty squares, hawkers banned.

Jacobs (1961) critiques from street level: visual order ≠ experienced order; function, not surface regularity, defines order; mixed use and complexity ('cross-use') are functionally superior; single-use zoning simplifies for planners. Planning as 'urban taxidermy': cities treated as works of art instead of living systems. Scott's wider point (ch. 9) is that high modernism ignores practical, local knowledge (mētis).
concepts: Faith in science/technology and state power to rationally redesign society and space.
Making society readable and controllable from the centre through simplification and standardisation.
Separating work, housing, leisure and traffic into zones.
Building a model city from scratch to demonstrate a new society.
Residents' 'disease' of anonymity and missing street life in Brasília.
Squatter and satellite settlements housing most people, symbiotic with the planned core.
Jacobs: tidy geometry ≠ a well-functioning, lived environment.
Practical, local, experience-based knowledge high modernism ignores.
example: Dutch post-war 'wijkgedachte' neighbourhoods (Bijlmermeer: high-rise, separated traffic levels) are a local high-modernist case, and its 1990s partial demolition a Jacobs-style correction.

examples.d: The construction workers (candangos) organised to claim land, services and title; by 1980, 75 percent of Brasília's population lived in settlements the plan never anticipated, while the planned city reached less than half its projected 557,000. Shows Scott's point that the legible, ordered centre depended on an unplanned city at the margins.

Le Corbusier replaced housing planned for the centre with an 'acropolis of monuments' on a 220-acre site, swapped crowded bazaars for huge squares that now stand largely empty, and street traders were banned from the centre. Shows functional segregation and order seen from above killing street life, again with an unplanned periphery.

Jacobs describes a housing project lawn that residents treated with contempt, because in a project of strangers they could not get a newspaper, a coffee or borrow fifty cents. Shows the gap between visual order and experienced, functional order.

Dense shops, bars and bakeries kept the North End busy all day, so shopkeepers, passers-by and elderly people at windows watched the street; on Jacobs's own street, neighbours and shopkeepers gathered to stop a possible abduction without any police. Shows informal, mixed-use order ('eyes on the street') that single-use planning cannot design.

title: Davoudi (2006) Evidence-based planning: rhetoric and reality
one: The UK enthusiasm for evidence-based policy rests on an instrumental, linear, utilitarian view of research, the same naive assumptions as 1960s–70s positivist planning. In the real world evidence competes with ideology, interests, institutions and prior information, so Davoudi argues for an enlightenment model: evidence-informed policy.
summary: Context: New Labour's Modernising Government White Paper (1999): 'what matters is what works'. Two models of the policy–research interface. The instrumental model (linear, direct) has two variants: 'expert on top' (research leads, evidence-driven policy) and 'expert on tap' (research follows policy concerns; speed, usable evidence on demand). The enlightenment model: indirect, long-term; research 'illuminates the landscape' and informs public debate, i.e. evidence-INFORMED rather than evidence-BASED policy.

The instrumental view rests on three misconceptions: policy-making is a rational process; evidence can only be generated by positive science; experts are apolitical and value-free, 'and they know best'. These echo planning history: Geddes' survey-analysis-plan (linear, but intuitive visionary planners); then 1960s–70s systems and rational planning (cybernetics, McLoughlin, Chadwick, location theory, Popper's falsifiability) which conceived planning as a science solving well-defined problems, 'the paradox of policy analysis'.

Real world: policy is bricolage (Ball); more information can confuse (Keynes); research sits on shelves ('problem of little effect', Weiss). Evidence competes with Weiss's four I's: ideology (e.g. urban containment/Green Belt sustained by values despite Hall's 1973 evidence), interests (DEFRA: evidence 'to turn strategic priorities into something concrete' → the political/tactical model, cherry-picking; think tanks under Thatcher; the Barker review), institutional norms and practices (quick fixes, unread reports), and prior information (facts only become evidence when used to support a proposition; evidence includes expert and experiential, formal and tacit knowledge; what counts is what is available; validity of relations matters). 'Power is knowledge' (Flyvbjerg): power determines what counts as knowledge.

The 2004 planning reform's 'soundness' test (PPS12: a 'robust and credible evidence base') became a largely procedural, tick-box exercise. Conclusion: the evidence-based enthusiasm and positivist planning share 'ambitious and naïve assumptions that the complex political and socio-economic processes could be technicized, commanded and controlled'. Keep a broad enlightenment view and two-way interaction between policy and research, and aim at an 'evidence-informed society'.
concepts: Linear, direct research→policy (expert on top) or policy→research (expert on tap).
Research indirectly illuminates the context and informs debate: evidence-informed policy.
Research leads policy / research serves policy demands.
Policy-making is rational; evidence only from positive science; experts are value-free and know best.
Ideology, interests, institutional norms/practices, prior information: competitors of evidence.
Evidence gathered or cherry-picked to justify decisions already made.
Facts become evidence only when used to (dis)prove a proposition; includes experiential and tacit knowledge.
UK 2004 plan test on a 'robust and credible evidence base'; in practice procedural, tick-box.
example: The Dutch MKBA/'onderbouwing' culture resembles the instrumental model; the fact that Green Heart and urban containment persist on values more than evidence illustrates Weiss's 'ideology'.

examples.d: DEFRA defined evidence as 'any information that helps turn DEFRA's strategic priorities into something concrete, manageable and achievable'. Shows Weiss's 'interests' and the political/tactical model: evidence is sought to justify priorities already decided.

Studies on the costs and benefits of high-density housing remained inconclusive and open to value-based readings, yet policy already treated high density as the route to sustainable communities. Shows that evidence is often incomplete or contested and that policy does not wait for it.

The 2004 English reform required plans to rest on a 'robust and credible evidence base', but early practice made soundness a procedural tick-box exercise rather than a test of which growth strategy is better. Shows evidence used in a quasi-judicial sense (reasoned justification) instead of substantive knowledge of how cities work.

A House of Commons report said of hazardous waste flows that 'no-one seems to have a clue what is going where', because strategic waste planning had not been treated as a policy problem worth research. Shows that 'research for policy's sake' is selective: evidence exists mainly where policy already looks.

title: Alexander: after rationality (contingency theory)
one: Rationality has broken down as planning's single paradigm, but nothing has replaced it. Alexander proposes a contingency framework: classic rationality (individual deliberation) and Habermas's communicative action (interaction) are mirror images, each valid in its own domain.
summary: Rationality plays two roles: a descriptive model (explaining decisions as if actors are rational) and a normative paradigm (analytic standard and prescription), and it remains the basis of planners' claims to expertise.

Responses to its breakdown: ritual (keep using it with token acknowledgment of anomalies), avoidance (swap in descriptive models such as Simon's satisficing or Lindblom's disjointed incrementalism), abandonment (drop process models for intuition, or for a substantive ideology such as neo-Marxism or public choice) and search (new paradigms, contingency models). The procedural-vs-substantive debate is sterile: it is really about level of abstraction (two dimensions: procedural↔structural focus; concrete↔abstract).

Critical theory/TCA (Habermas) adds reflexive consciousness and the shift from decision to interaction, but it is normative, procedural, and ignores the pre-interactive deliberation by which actors decide what to pursue. Most real interaction is strategic, not communicative. Rationality ignores interaction; TCA ignores deliberation. 'One paradigm cannot supplant another', so a contingency framework combines them.

Lecture use: rationality is 'no more than a more sophisticated word for reason' (Alexander 2000, 4): having reasons (linking means to ends) and giving reasons (justification). The midterm example question also quotes Alexander's institutional design: 'the deliberate creation of institutions by planners to achieve politically defined societal goals', which Moroni criticises (week 4).
concepts: Different models are valid under different conditions; a framework assigns domains.
Oriented to consensus through argument vs to success through power and manipulation.
Devising rules, procedures and organisational structures to achieve held values/objectives; at macro, meso and micro levels.
example: A municipality internally ranks options with an MCA (deliberation, rational), then negotiates with developers and residents (interaction, strategic or communicative).

examples.d: Alexander notes that much planning education and practice keeps following the rational model with only token acknowledgement of its anomalies. Illustrates why rationality survives as the normative basis of planners' claims to expertise even after the paradigm broke down.

Mediation, conflict resolution and arbitration belong in the real, collective, consensus-oriented cell only when carried out by a neutral participant or a consensus-oriented group, which Alexander calls rare; once actors pursue their own goals, the same process is strategic action (bargaining, negotiation). Shows how the contingency framework sorts one practice by the actor's purpose.

Formal optimisation such as linear programming and multi-objective decision-making sits in the ideal, individual cell, while satisficing, disjointed incrementalism and mixed scanning describe how individuals actually decide (real, individual cell). Shows the ideal/real split: rationality works as a norm, not as a description.

title: Rational choice & self-interest (lecture) + Coase
one: All actors (citizens, developers, municipalities) maximise self-interest; property rights and institutions shape their incentives. Planning faces both market failure and state failure, and can work by clarifying rights and cutting transaction costs.
summary: Rational-comprehensive planning is an ideal standard for planning decisions (expert, value-free welfare optimisation). Rational choice theory is an analytical framework for how planning works: rational decision-making by ALL actors, market and state failure, emulating market rationality in state processes.

Public interest has no objective, universal goal; it is the aggregate of private interests (agency-focused). Land-use planning is limited: landowners have a de facto veto ('Land-use planning will only succeed if it can influence private decisions', Needham 2012, p. 24). Rent = income from owning land above the cost of production (Ricardo). Asymmetry: when planning raises land values owners keep the betterment; when it lowers them (downzoning, heritage, regulatory takings) they claim compensation. Landowner strategies (Rijnenburg, Buitelaar et al. 2025): framing ('low-hanging fruit'), collaborating (consortium), lobbying, negotiating. Swiss hypothesis: the peasant land law bars outsiders buying farmland and caps price gains, so there is no speculative expansion lobby and insiders gain from densification.

Airbnb: incentives differ (hosts, guests, neighbours, planners). Under-regulation is a collective action problem (Olson): small concentrated interests organise; large diffuse groups free-ride. Regulation (Utrecht 2018: 60 nights, guest cap, registration, fines €150–€21,750) suffers from enforcement, data, transaction costs, legal challenges and waterbed effects. Coase (1960): with clearly defined property rights and zero transaction costs, bargaining yields the efficient outcome regardless of who holds the right. Since transaction costs are never zero (information, bargaining, enforcement, holdouts, many parties), design Coasean interventions: clarify rights and cut transaction costs (tradable hosting permits, VvE negotiation, hosting tax into a neighbourhood fund, platform monitoring).

Core assumptions: self-interest maximisation (not only economic); applies to all actors; property rights/institutions shape incentives and can be deliberately changed; outcomes judged in costs and benefits; knowledge mostly positivist (models, game theory, CBA). Can explain reproduction (insiders protect interests) and transformation (deliberate redesign of rules). Critiques: over-simple human model, ignores power and inequality, too agency-focused, limiting assumptions, reverse nirvana fallacy.
concepts: Actors weigh costs and benefits to pursue their own interests (not only money).
Government also fails: rent-seeking, capture, information and incentive problems.
Effect of one actor's action on others not reflected in prices (noise, safety, housing pressure).
Individually rational free-riding leads to collectively suboptimal outcomes.
Clear property rights + zero transaction costs → efficient bargaining outcome, whoever holds the right.
Information, bargaining, enforcement, strategic behaviour (holdouts), many parties.
Unearned income from land; efforts to capture it via the political process.
Owners keep planning gains but claim planning losses.
Public regulation that reduces the value of private property.
example: Airbnb in Amsterdam: hosts form a small, concentrated, organised interest; neighbours are a large, diffuse group who free-ride, so regulation lags.

examples.d: Quiet is worth €1,000 to the homeowner and insulation costs the factory €700; whoever holds the right, bargaining leads to insulation and only who pays whom changes. Shows Coase's theorem, which holds only if rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are zero.

Utrecht set a limit of 60 nights a year, a guest cap per m2, a registration number, a reporting duty and fines from €150 to €21,750. Rational choice scholars expect such one-size-fits-all rules to struggle with detection, platforms withholding data, enforcement transaction costs and waterbed effects.

Bouwmeester's hypothesis: Swiss law (BGBB) blocks farmland sales at more than 5-15 percent above agricultural value and bars non-farmers from buying farmland, so no speculative outsider lobby pushes for expansion and insider owners gain scarcity rents from inward growth. Shows property rules shaping incentives so that supporting densification becomes the rational strategy.

Dutch owners can claim compensation (planschade, under the Omgevingswet 'nadeelcompensatie') when a new plan lowers their property's value, while value gains from upzoning are not taxed as such. A close case of the asymmetry on the slides: landowners keep betterment but claim planning damages.

title: Needham (2012) Interests and rights in property
theory: Institutional economics of property rights (law and economics; rational choice lens in the course)
one: Land-use planning is not the public interest against the market: it is one of two ways the state protects identifiable private interests in land, the other being property rights enforced by their holders in court. Which interests get which protection is a political and technical choice that can be revised, so some planning goals could be reached by creating markets in property rights; Needham finds this feasible only under limited circumstances.
summary: Reframing (pp. 23–26): planning is usually justified by 'the public interest', which Needham rejects: it is hard to substantiate, economic 'distortion' arguments no longer convince, and it depersonalises: 'But we too are the public!' People have interests in how land is used, their own and their neighbours' (a deep hole, a pink door, traffic, shops, open landscape, clean air). The authority upholds 'the identifiable interests of many identifiable private persons'. Planning is also not 'command and control': owners' decisions remain voluntary, and 'Land-use planning will succeed only if it can influence the private decisions' (p. 24), via permits, subsidies/levies, persuasion or infrastructure; only taking ownership removes the decision.

Rights (pp. 26–28): ownership is never absolute; owners may not seriously harm others (though many countries allow harm if the benefit exceeds it, Coase), and owners can grant partial rights (a lease). A property right is a way of using land 'recognized by, and protected by, the courts', so rights are created by the state, not natural (against Locke): 'It is the fact that something is protected that makes it a right' (Bromley). The state protects interests in two ways: private law (the interest becomes a property right the holder enforces in court) and public law (a public authority such as a municipality restricts how others use their rights, e.g. via building permits). Which route applies is partly political (the door colour is not protected at all) and partly technical (right of support: clear cause and few parties; clean air: diffuse effects, hundreds of victims who cannot organise a lawsuit, so public law).

Rights as policy variable (pp. 28–29): because the split is a decision, it can be revised; property rights can 'be deliberately changed in order purposefully to influence land use', although rights carry high ideological content and the ECHR limits change. Example: vesting future generations' interests as rights held by trustees. A market exists when there is a wanted good, voluntary exchange with free choice of partner, and regular exchange (Hodgson). As markets cannot be excluded (Lindblom), 'planning or the market?' is the wrong question; it is about the mix (Buitelaar), and moving protection from public to private law means creating markets in property rights.

Method and cases (pp. 30–34): Coase's reciprocity ('Should A be allowed to harm B or should B be allowed to harm A?'), Ellickson's alternatives to zoning and Webster & Lai's club goods. Needham distinguishes this from libertarian attacks on planning, keeps the planning goals, and compares instruments by effectiveness ('remediability', Williamson), not by assumed efficiency. Four cases: housing-estate amenity via covenants and a residents' association (US, England; not binding in the Netherlands); industrial estates maintained by one investor-landlord (not possible in NL: no compulsory association, leases not tradable, so estates decay and need public money; fix: make unexpired leases saleable); privately owned public spaces under permit conditions; and regional coherence, where effects are too dispersed for a market, though US conservation agreements buy development rights.

Conclusions (pp. 34–35): creating markets in property rights is feasible 'only under certain limited circumstances', and feasibility is not desirability. Advantages: less inflexible, no public compensation for 'takings'; risks: exclusive developments such as gated communities and urban fragmentation. Politically neither left nor right: with Blomley, Needham argues poorer people can be empowered by giving them rights in property. Course framing (HC6): rational choice can explain transformation through deliberate redesign of rights, while Taylor shows reproduction by insiders.
concepts: What a person wants regarding how any land is used (own or others'); only some interests are protected, as rights or by planning (pp. 25–28).
'A way of using land (and buildings), where that way is recognized by, and protected by, the courts' (p. 27); created by the state, never absolute.
The state makes an interest a property right; the holder takes the violator to court on her own initiative (p. 27).
A public authority uses powers (permits, prohibitions) to protect those who cannot protect their interests otherwise: land-use planning (pp. 27–28).
Whether an interest is protected at all is political; whether as right or by regulation depends on clarity of cause–effect and number of parties (p. 28).
Since rights are created, they can be deliberately changed to steer land use, like land tenure reform (pp. 28–29).
Something wanted; voluntary exchange with free choice of partner; regular exchange among more people (p. 29).
Restricting A to protect B harms A; the question is who may harm whom (p. 30).
Williamson's approach: compare how effectively alternative instruments reach the same policy goal, not maximum efficiency (p. 30).
Shifting protection from public law to private law, creating exchange structures in which people realise planning goals themselves (pp. 29–31).
example: Dutch industrial estates (p. 32): firms that own their buildings cannot be obliged to join an association that maintains shared spaces, and tenants avoid long leases because an unexpired lease cannot be sold on. So nobody holds the rights needed to protect the shared interest in quality, estates deteriorate quickly, and only large amounts of public money improve them. In England/US one investor-landlord holds the rights and maintains the estate to protect his investment.

examples.d: In the US (private community associations) and less often England, buyers sign covenants against changes that harm the estate and a residents' association enforces them; in the Netherlands this is not legally binding because owners cannot be obliged to join such an association. Shows an interest turned into a property right, and how national property law decides whether a market alternative to planning exists.

A neighbour damaging my foundations is covered by a property right (the right of support) because cause, culprit and victim are clear and few; clean air is protected by public law (permits, emission limits) because effects are diffuse and hundreds of victims cannot organise a court case. Shows the partly technical, partly political choice between private-law and public-law protection of interests.

Shopping malls, and small housing developments where residents own and maintain shared spaces that stay open to all, operate under planning conditions on public access and maintenance. Shows property rights deliberately created to deliver a certain type of urban environment.

A public or private trust buys a farmer's development rights and never uses them, so the land stays open while the farmer keeps ownership. Shows a public planning goal pursued with private-law tools where regional interests are too dispersed for a market in rights.

title: Hindmoor (2006) Mancur Olson and the logic of collective action
one: Collective goods are non-excludable, so each rational, self-interested member may free-ride and the good goes under-provided: a collective action problem, best modelled as an (N-person) prisoners' dilemma. Olson does not claim collective action is impossible; groups overcome the problem through coercion, privileged members, selective incentives, process benefits, or conditional cooperation. The self-interest assumption and the lack of a full theory of group formation limit the account.
summary: The problem (pp. 102–105): Olson (1965) challenged the assumption that people with common interests will act on them: 'unless the number of individuals is quite small, or there is coercion or some other special device', self-interested individuals will not act for their group interest. Goods are classed by excludability and rivalness (Box 5.1): public goods (defence), common-pool goods (fisheries), toll goods, private goods. Olson defines public goods only by non-excludability, so the problem covers common goods too. Examples: union dues, Marxist revolution (why risk the barricades?), pluralists such as Truman and Bentley (latent groups like migrant workers may never form), CO2 emissions, the security dilemma.

Game theory (pp. 105–112; Olson himself used none): the prisoners' dilemma (Jake and Keith) has a dominant strategy of defection and a Pareto-inferior equilibrium; the N-person version (join a protest or stay home) shows free-riding. Not every collective action problem is a PD: in the assurance game (the dam needs both farmers) there is no dominant strategy and cooperation should be easy; in chicken (either farmer can fix the dam) each tries to make the other do it, and 'anything can happen'.

Solutions (pp. 113–121): Olson 'does not suggest that groups will always fail'. (1) Coercion by the state (taxes; Hardin's leviathan for the tragedy of the commons, against which free-market economists propose property rights and tradeable permits based on Coase) or by gangs (Gambetta's Mafia enforcing exchange). (2) Privileged groups: at least one member values the good enough to pay the whole cost (flatmate who cleans; hegemonic stability); several such members can turn it into chicken. (3) Selective incentives: positive (union legal aid) or negative (ostracism); they raise a second-order collective action problem, possibly solved by entrepreneurs. (4) Process benefits: participation itself is rewarding (Chong on civil rights; kibbutz gossip). (5) Conditional cooperation in intermediate groups, where members notice who contributes: tit-for-tat won Axelrod's tournaments; Ostrom shows communities manage commons without leviathan or market when interaction is long-term, exit is costly, monitoring is cheap and groups are tightly integrated.

Group size (p. 121): large groups are more likely to be latent, because contributions are easier to see in small groups, but the link is 'at most, an empirical tendency' (a mining community vs strangers in a bed-sit). Limits (pp. 122–128): people also contribute because norms say they ought to; Olson concedes his theory cannot explain 'non-economic' groups like Greenpeace or Amnesty. Experiments (Marwell & Ames) find substantial group contributions that fall, but stay positive, when stakes rise; a few unconditional cooperators may be needed to pass the threshold at which cooperation becomes stable. Assessment: Olson was the first to give a general analysis and inspired many case studies, but he offers no comprehensive theory of how interests and group identities form, how platforms are agreed, how collective action changes policy, or why groups collapse; social psychology and insider-group research are needed too.

Course application (HC6, not in the chapter): Airbnb regulation lags because hosts/investors organise while neighbours free-ride. Hindmoor's chapter supports the free-riding part, but warns that size is only a tendency and that small groups organise when one member gains enough (privileged) or when members can monitor each other (intermediate). The link with Needham: diffuse harms such as air pollution cannot be protected by individual property rights because victims cannot organise to sue.
concepts: All members gain if they act together, but no individual gains from contributing to the collective good: free-riding (p. 102).
Classified by excludability and rivalness (Box 5.1); Olson's definition uses non-excludability only, so common-pool goods face the problem too.
Game where defection is the dominant strategy and the equilibrium is Pareto-inferior to mutual cooperation (pp. 105–110).
Collective action games without a dominant strategy: assurance (both needed, cooperation easy); chicken (one suffices, each waits for the other) (pp. 110–112).
Latent: nobody bears their share; privileged: at least one member will pay the full cost (Olson 1965: 48–50); intermediate: members notice whether others contribute (Olson 1965: 50).
Excludable rewards for contributors (e.g. free legal representation) or punishments for non-contributors (e.g. ostracism) (Olson 1965: 133–5).
Applying selective incentives (e.g. punishing free-riders) is itself a collective good, risking an infinite regress (pp. 116–117).
Instrumental or expressive rewards from participating itself; tied to the collective good, so the problem 'simply dissolves' (pp. 117–118).
Cooperate as long as others do; in iterated games tit-for-tat wins on average via simplicity, generosity, responsiveness (pp. 118–120).
Communities build rules of allocation, monitoring and sanctioning for common-pool resources without a leviathan or the market (p. 120).
example: Ostrom's Valencia irrigation system (p. 121): it is designed so that the person whose turn is next has a built-in incentive to check that the current user does not take more than their share, lowering monitoring costs so conditional cooperation can last without state coercion or privatisation. Course application (HC6): short-term rental hosts organise while neighbours free-ride, so regulation lags.

examples.d: Keeping the flat clean is a potential collective action problem, but if one student hates squalor enough to clean alone, the others can free-ride and the good is still provided. Shows Olson's 'privileged group'.

Workers may join a union for free legal representation (positive selective incentive) or to avoid being ostracised, 'sent to Coventry' (negative incentive). Hindmoor adds that this still leaves a second-order problem: who organised the union or does the ostracising in the first place?

Members get housing and food regardless of effort, yet work hard because shirkers become targets of vicious gossip, and gossiping is enjoyable in itself. Shows process benefits solving the second-order problem, helped by the fact that leaving a kibbutz is hard.

examples.t: Cooperation in First World War trenches
examples.d: Soldiers facing each other for long periods evolved norms such as firing only at set times, once even playing football on Christmas day; commanders then rotated troops to erode that trust. Shows conditional cooperation needs stable membership and repeated interaction.

title: Taylor (2016) Urban growth boundaries and betterment: rent-seeking in Melbourne
one: Analysing 264 public submissions on Melbourne's 2010 UGB expansion and the Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution (a betterment tax), Taylor shows that landowners as 'insiders' rent-sought successfully: they discredited expected windfalls and got the GAIC shifted to purchasers, so costs are passed on to homebuyers ('outsiders').
summary: Melbourne's UGB (2002) expanded substantially in 2010; land inside rose 89% per hectare relative to comparable land outside, creating 'instant millionaires'. The GAIC was a hypothecated per-hectare tax on the expected betterment, to fund infrastructure.

Landowners have multiple interests: premium-seeking owners (often broadacre farmers, vacant land) want inclusion and to unlock development value, and containment creates speculation through 'dual predictability' (Nelson). Others, affluent rural-residential 'lifestyle' owners and hobby farmers, want to preserve restrictions for amenity and value stability ('homevoters', Fischel). Among submissions: 33 included owners were happy, 11 wanted to stay rural; 52 excluded owners wanted inclusion; grassland-zone owners called protection 'conning landowners from their rights'.

Landowners framed the GAIC as 'unbelievable, unethical, outright robbery', disputed that betterment would occur (a 'Taxed Out!' campaign), and argued it should be paid by developers/buyers. 'Landowner-led pressure on policy makers ultimately led to a set of modifications to the GAIC bill' (p. 272): exemptions for small parcels (0.41–5 ha, ~56% of liable parcels), liability shifted to purchasers (30% at purchase, rest at development), and in 2011 fully deferred to development, which protected hobby farmers.

Conclusion: the outcome legitimised landowners' misinterpretation of development gain; representations of self-interest were taken 'at face value as more equitable'. Policies 'are decided in large part on the basis of whether or not they survive conflict with groups with an existing economic stake'. Containment creates land premiums that are redistributed through the lobbying of 'insiders', with costs passed to housing consumers ('outsiders'). Rent-seeking by existing owners can decide whether and how strategic planning is implemented.
concepts: Legislated line separating urban from non-urban land.
Land-value increase caused by public action; here the windfall from the UGB shift.
Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution: hypothecated betterment tax, later made 'purchaser pays'.
Lobbying to capture or keep unearned rents.
Owners wanting development value vs owners protecting amenity and property value through restrictions.
Containment makes clear which land can be developed AND that it is scarce, fuelling speculation.
Existing property owners who capture gains vs future homebuyers who pay.
example: Rijnenburg (Utrecht): developer-owned land was framed as 'low-hanging fruit' for housing, lobbying against the energy-landscape vision.

examples.d: Rural land around Melbourne worth $15,000 to $35,000 per hectare averaged $365,000 once inside the UGB and rezoned, and after the 2010 shift prices inside rose 89 percent relative to comparable land outside. Shows betterment, an unearned increment created by planning, which the GAIC ($95,000 per hectare) aimed to tax.

21 owners whose land in the west was to become protected grassland called the rules unfair and wanted in, while hobby farmers argued to keep green wedge restrictions protecting their amenity. Shows Taylor's two rent-seeking interests: premium-seeking to unlock development value versus homevoters defending restrictions.

examples.t: Owners with development plans stayed quiet
examples.d: Only 4 of 49 landowners with development plans objected to the GAIC, against 72 of 137 without such plans. Those who knew their development value saw the charge as small against the gain; opposition came from owners who framed it as a tax on existing value.

The Taxed Out! campaign cast the GAIC as a tax on existing land value; the bill was redrafted to exempt 0.41 to 5 hectare parcels (about 56 percent of liable parcels) and shift liability to purchasers, and in 2011 fully deferred to development. Shows insiders shifting the cost of value capture onto outsiders, future homebuyers.

title: Neo-institutionalism: the map
one: Institutions are the formal and informal rules of the game, not organisations. They are 'ontologically both the context and object of planning' (Savini 2019). New institutionalism comes as rational choice, sociological, historical and evolutionary strands, which disagree on what institutions are, what they do and how they change, and so on how much planners can deliberately design them.
summary: Institutions = systems of established rules and norms that guide, constrain and regulate behaviour; organisations = concrete entities with a purpose (Eurovision: EBU = organisation; statutes and informal norms = institutions). Double life: they constrain actors but are also outcomes of action (context AND object of planning). Alexander (2005): if planning aims to transform society, 'institutional transformation must be a critical aspect of planning'. Some even say 'planning is institutional design' (Innes 1995): planners → design institutions → shape behaviour → reshape society/space.

Origins (Part A): Hardin's tragedy of the commons (1968): rational self-interest depletes shared resources. Ostrom (1990) shows how self-interested people self-organise rules to overcome the 'problem of commitment'. Her IAD framework has seven rule types: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, payoff, scope (applied to informal real estate by Bouwmeester & Hartmann 2021). New institutionalism explains how institutions shape behaviour and how they arise and change, and reconciles structure and agency (Giddens). Example: institutional arrangements shape residential morphology in NL, Flanders and NRW (Tennekes et al. 2015).

Strands (Part B, after Sorensen 2017 and Salet 2018). (1) Rational choice institutionalism: 'formal and informal rules of the game … humanly devised constraints' (North 1990); they coordinate and give certainty, information and credible commitment; they change when self-interested actors create rules to enhance cooperation. (2) Sociological: institutions 'establish the very criteria by which people discover their preferences'; goodness-of-fit with legitimate templates (DiMaggio & Powell); symbol systems, cognitive scripts, moral templates (Hall & Taylor); internalised; hegemonic norms. Example: Amsterdam-Noord's symbols linking the shipyard past to a creative future (Savini & Dembski 2016). (3) Historical: procedures, routines and norms embedded in the polity; path dependency, critical junctures, structural emphasis. Example: why participation in Norwegian land-use planning stayed weak (Holsen 2021). (4) Evolutionary (Moroni): institutions as unintended outcomes of evolution.

The key debate is institutional change and the limits of design. Dembski & Salet: symbols can't be used voluntaristically; find under-institutionalised niches. Sorensen: critical junctures, then bounded developmental pathways. Moroni: emergent institutions can't be designed like organisations, so a kosmos approach. 'How we conceptualize institutions shapes how we conceptualize planning agency.'
