examples.d: The New Deal combined counselling to raise self-esteem with training to build skills. Raco and Imrie cite it as a 'technology of citizenship': empowerment used to turn powerless subjects into active, self-governing citizens who take responsibility for their own welfare.

Best Value required councils to adopt new disciplines of value for money and efficiency, with central action if they failed to act 'responsibly'; Best Practice guidelines made SRB bidders adjust their conduct to the scrutiny of other bidders. Governing at a distance: discipline that works through self-monitoring and peers rather than direct central orders.

DETR guidance on tenant participation calls for a 'proper balance of rights and responsibilities', but tenants who gain a say must follow public service rules and accept the council's ultimate responsibility for strategic decisions. Communities of obligation: rights to take part come bundled with centrally defined duties.

In the 2013 King's Speech the Dutch government announced a shift from the welfare state to a 'participatiesamenleving', in which citizens are expected to take more responsibility for their own lives and neighbourhoods. A close Dutch analogue of the rights and responsibilities agenda and the governmentality of active citizenship.

title: Gurran & Ruming (2016) Less planning, more development? Housing and urban reform discourses in Australia
theory: Discourse analysis (broadly Foucauldian: regimes of truth) within a critique of neoliberal planning reform
one: In the 2011–2014 New South Wales planning reform, the development industry's framing of planning as 'red tape' that blocks housing supply, growth and affordability became a 'regime of truth' that the government's White Paper and draft Planning Bill largely adopted, while community, environmental and affordable-housing concerns were sidelined. Housing affordability served as a 'semantic justification' for a wider deregulatory agenda; the Bill nevertheless stalled under community backlash, and approvals boomed while prices kept rising.
summary: Context (pp. 1–7). Planning systems have resisted deregulation and elsewhere (UK section 106, US inclusionary zoning) are used to secure affordable housing, but their legitimacy is now questioned for slowing supply (Glaeser and Ward, Ball) and for exclusionary use by owners. Australia has one of the world's most expensive housing markets; ownership fell from about 71% (mid-1980s) to 68% (2012). A long-running national microeconomic reform agenda (COAG) prioritises deregulation of planning and development assessment. Social housing approvals in NSW fell from around 15% of dwellings in 1983 to under 2% in July 2014; the NHSC's 85,000-dwelling shortfall would have been roughly offset (90,000 extra dwellings) had social housing production stayed at its 1996 level (p. 6).

Approach (pp. 2–3, 7–9). A 'broadly Foucauldian analysis' treats language as producing reality: the power of a group rests on its capacity to sustain a version of reality as 'objective truth'; discourses harden into 'regimes of truth' that fix acceptable problems and solutions (Jacobs, Hastings, Clapham). Data: the July 2012 Green Paper (over 1,200 submissions, 72% from community individuals and organisations, 1% from the development industry), 13 selected submissions (industry: PCA, UDIA, Urban Taskforce, Australand, HIA, Master Builders; plus PIA, LGSA, WSROC, Shelter NSW, EDO, NCC/TEC, and the resident group FOKE), and the April 2013 White Paper and draft Planning Bill; close reading, coding and NVIVO keyword searches.

Findings: framing and objectives (pp. 10–11). Industry frames planning as dysfunctional, bureaucratic and anti-growth, and residents as part of the problem; local government and residents frame the problem as distrust and 'undue influence of developers'. PCA: the system should deliver 'an economic dividend'. Local government and residents want ecologically sustainable development, social impact and heritage objectives kept. The White Paper makes promoting economic growth the 'main purpose' of planning; the Bill positions housing as 'economic activity' and relegates environment and society through 'while' and 'having regard to'.

Findings: specific reforms (pp. 11–14). Easier spot rezoning with developer appeals: supported by industry, opposed by councils, adopted. Participation: promised as central, yet no new consultation rights and curtailed statutory consultation in development assessment; Australand wants an 'antidevelopment culture' to shift. Red tape: PCA's claim of 40% cost reduction comes with no evidence; the Bill bans 'onerous' controls affecting financial viability. Infrastructure: here government resists industry, which (against its free-market line) wants broad-based public funding; developers keep paying. Affordable housing: Shelter's inclusionary zoning ignored; existing affordable housing contribution provisions are wound back.

Conclusion (pp. 14–16). Industry discourse aligned with neoliberal ideology dominated the formal process, but ideology and interests are not the only drivers: the Bill stalled by the end of 2013 in parliament, where the government lacked a majority, after a backlash by the Better Planning Network (more than 300 resident groups; the 'Hazzard tape' protest), whose influence worked outside the formal process. Ironically, approvals reached a 20-year high and almost doubled (Dec 2011 to 2014) under the unreformed system, while Sydney's median house price rose from $535,000 (March 2011) to $735,000 (December 2014): more supply did not ease affordability. The authors ask whether reform discourse distracts from the real pressures on low-income renters and aspiring owners.
concepts: Language as producing reality and knowledge, not a neutral medium; meaning is contested and tied to power.
A dominant, relatively static representation of reality that fixes which problems and solutions count as acceptable (Foucault 1980, via Jacobs).
The industry narrative that planning regulation constrains supply, raises costs and so causes unaffordability; deregulation is the cure.
Using housing affordability as a rhetorical warrant for deregulation whose real content is growth and development.
Placing environmental and social goals in subordinate clauses ('while', 'having regard to') so that growth becomes the primary purpose.
Microeconomic reform aimed at deregulation and competition: simplified controls, faster decisions, standardised plans, user-pays infrastructure.
Changing permissible land uses on a single site; can deliver large windfalls; the reform eased it and allowed developer appeals.
Levying the value uplift from upzoning to fund affordable housing or infrastructure; proposed by Shelter and PIA, not adopted.
Australian term for growth management: containing greenfield spread and densifying existing areas; opposed by both industry (land supply) and residents (density).
example: The PCA claimed the new system should 'reduce costs by 40% by 2015' through red-tape reduction; the authors note 'no evidence of actual costs or savings is ever provided', yet the draft Bill (s3.3, Principle 10) bars local plans from 'overly complex or onerous controls that may adversely impact on the financial viability of proposed development' (p. 12).

examples.t: The shortage that social housing explains
examples.d: In 2008 the National Housing Supply Council estimated a shortfall of about 85,000 dwellings, yet also found that keeping social housing output at its 1996 level would have added about 90,000, a modest surplus. This undercuts the industry's 'regime of truth' that planning red tape is the main cause of the shortage.

Shelter NSW proposed levying developers for affordable housing where rezoning creates value uplift, but the draft Planning Bill actually cut existing affordable housing contribution provisions. The authors conclude affordability served as a 'semantic justification' for deregulation rather than a real policy aim.

The Better Planning Network, a coalition of over 300 resident groups and local government representatives, wrapped Planning Minister Brad Hazzard in yellow 'Hazzard' tape, and by the end of 2013 the Bill stalled in parliament. Shows that the industry's discursive dominance inside formal consultation could still be blocked by electoral power and direct action outside it.

Under the unreformed planning system NSW housing approvals reached a 20-year high, almost doubling between December 2011 and 2014, while Sydney's median house price still rose from $535,000 to $735,000. Evidence against the claim that planning blocks supply and that more supply alone restores affordability.
